terra.problem: The woman calls herself the king’s maidservant, so servants do come up in her story.
The woman’s story does not say how old her son is; calling him a young man adds a detail.
The explanation states David’s thoughts and says nobody warned him, neither of which the text establishes.
It states that the woman is a widow as fact, though that is part of the story Joab told her to present.
The text does not say that the woman’s mourning clothes remain on during this exchange.
The passage does not establish that Absalom is closer to David than he has been in years.
The passage gives the trip’s destination, but it does not establish that Bethlehem was not a stop along the way.
Absalom’s plan is not the only thing that changes afterward: his servants set Joab’s field on fire, and Joab comes to him.
The text says the servants set the field on fire, but it does not say that nobody gathered anything.
Geshur is a kingdom or region, not a town like Tekoa.
Absalom asks to see the king and says that if there is iniquity in him, the king should kill him. The explanation turns those into alternatives and leaves out the condition.
Absalom does not ask for a meeting or a verdict as alternatives. He asks to see the king and makes a separate conditional statement about being killed.
